newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila backs Amari deal but wants "renegotiation".
newsitem.headline: Manila backs Amari deal but wants "renegotiation".

text.p: The Philippine presidential palace upheld on Saturday a controversial land deal between a government agency and the Amari Coastal Bay Development Corp but ordered a renegotiation of certain provisions of the contract.

Presidential Executive Secretary Ruben Torres said the joint venture agreement between the Public Estates Authority (PEA) and Amari "has been found to be valid" based on the recommendations of a presidential fact-finding committee that reviewed the deal.
The committee last month endorsed the deal but said "corrections" would have to be made in the contract.

Torres directed PEA to "clarify and renegotiate such provisions in the joint venture agreement which give the impression of a sale or disposition of government property to reflect its true intent and spirit as a joint venture agreement."
The final agreement will be submitted to the Office of the President for review and final approval, he said in a statement.
The deal involved the reclamation and development of 750 hectares of land in Manila.
Amari, a joint venture between Centennial City Inc and Ital-Thai Development Plc secured the Manila Bay contract from PEA last year.
Senate president Ernesto Maceda has said the PEA entered into a disadvantageous deal, alleging the property was grossly undervalued.
Guoco Holdings (Phils) Inc, parent company of Centennial, defended the deal, saying the valuation of 1,250 pesos per square metre was based on appraisals made by three independent firms.
Budget Secretary and committee head Salvador Enriquez last week said some PEA officials might have benefited from the deal.

Torres, in a memorandum released by the palace, directed the Securities and Exchange Commission to look into "the corporate transactions and/or corporate reorganisations (of Amari) with respect to the land deal." It did not elaborate.

He also ordered the fact-finding committee to submit to state prosecutors its findings so that they can determine if there was "probable criminal liability" and "administrative culpability" of certain PEA officials."
